TargetHeightCalculator.guideTitle: How to estimate a child’s adult height
TargetHeightCalculator.intro: This free height calculator uses the mid-parental method, also called the target-height or Tanner method. It combines the measured heights of the biological parents with a conventional adjustment for the child’s sex. The answer is a starting point for discussing family height patterns, rather than a forecast of exactly how tall a child will become.
TargetHeightCalculator.step1: Measure the biological father’s and mother’s adult heights without shoes. Use recent measurements when available rather than an approximate height remembered from years ago.
TargetHeightCalculator.step2: Select centimeters or inches and enter both heights in that unit. For example, 5 feet 10 inches is 70 inches; do not enter 5.10 as a decimal height.
TargetHeightCalculator.step3: Confirm the child’s sex and calculate the family target. Optionally add the child’s age, measured height and previous measurements for the CDC chart. Changing any input requires a new calculation.
TargetHeightCalculator.formulaExplanation: The adjustment is inside the parentheses: 13 cm is added or subtracted before dividing by two. Equivalently, calculate the parents’ average height and then add 6.5 cm for a boy or subtract 6.5 cm for a girl. The same metric formula is used when you enter inches, so changing units does not select a different method.
TargetHeightCalculator.workedTitle: Worked example: father 178 cm, mother 165 cm
TargetHeightCalculator.workedBoy: For a boy: (178 + 165 + 13) ÷ 2 = 178 cm. The conventional target range is 169.5–186.5 cm.
TargetHeightCalculator.workedGirl: For a girl with the same parental heights: (178 + 165 − 13) ÷ 2 = 165 cm. The conventional target range is 156.5–173.5 cm.
TargetHeightCalculator.rangeTitle: What does the target range mean?
TargetHeightCalculator.rangeExplanation: The calculator shows the target plus and minus 8.5 cm, following the clinical reference linked below. It describes a conventional family-based range, not an individual probability forecast. Published methods can use different adjustments or ranges. Real adult height can fall outside this interval, and the decimal shown in the result is calculation precision, not prediction accuracy.
TargetHeightCalculator.limitsTitle: What this height predictor cannot tell you
TargetHeightCalculator.limitsText: The family target calculation does not use the child’s age or current height. The optional chart compares entered heights with the CDC reference and can illustrate a constant-percentile scenario. Neither method evaluates puberty, bone age, growth remaining or the need for treatment. Nutrition, health conditions and puberty timing can affect final height.
TargetHeightCalculator.consultText: If you are concerned about growth, take repeated measurements and discuss them with a pediatrician. A clinician can consider the growth chart and medical history and decide whether further assessment is appropriate. Do not use a low or high estimate on its own to label a child’s growth or start supplements or medication.

accuracy.q: Can this calculator predict exactly how tall my child will be?
accuracy.a: No. It estimates a family-based target and a conventional range. An individual child may finish growing above or below that range. A single calculated value cannot capture all the factors involved in growth.

age.q: Do I need my child’s age or current height?
age.a: Not for the family target formula: it uses parental heights and sex. You can optionally enter the child’s age and current measured height for the CDC height-for-age chart, for ages 2–20. These measurements do not change the family target.

missing.q: What if I do not know one biological parent’s height?
missing.a: This calculator needs both heights. Do not enter a population average or a nonbiological caregiver’s height as a substitute and treat the answer as a personal estimate. Ask your pediatrician about assessing growth with the information available.

boneAge.q: Is target height the same as a bone-age prediction?
boneAge.a: No. This tool uses family heights and does not assess bone maturity. Bone-age assessment uses additional clinical information and imaging interpreted by a professional. No X-ray is needed to use this simple calculator.

units.q: Can I enter feet and inches?
units.a: Select inches and first convert the full height: multiply feet by 12 and add the remaining inches. For example, 5 feet 5 inches is 65 inches. The calculator converts this to centimeters for the formula.

growth.q: Does the result show whether my child is short for their age?
growth.a: The family target refers to adulthood. If you add the child’s measurements, the chart shows their height percentile for age and sex, including whether it is below P3 or above P97 in the CDC reference. That position alone does not diagnose a condition or confirm healthy growth.

table.q: What does the yearly height table show?
table.a: It shows CDC height-for-age references for each completed year from 2 to 20, including the 3rd, 50th and 97th percentiles for the selected sex. Optional illustration values are clearly separated from measured heights. You can hover, tap or focus a row to inspect the same age on the chart.

growth.title: Height by age: measurements and reference curves
growth.intro: See yearly height references and where your child’s measurements fall. Family target height describes adulthood; it is not a height target for each childhood year.
growth.below: Below P3 in this reference. Confirm the measurement and discuss it with a pediatrician, especially if the child is dropping across percentiles.
growth.within: Between P3 and P97 in this reference. This position alone cannot confirm healthy growth; changes over time and clinical context matter.
growth.above: Above P97 in this reference. Confirm the measurement and discuss any concerns or changes in the growth pattern with a pediatrician.
growth.familyComparison: Family height and the illustrative scenario
growth.familyReminder: Adult family target: {value}. Conventional adult range: {lower}–{upper}. Do not compare today’s childhood height directly with this adult range.
growth.endpoint: If the current percentile stayed the same, the reference at age 20 would be approximately {value}.
growth.belowFamily: This scenario falls below the family target range.
growth.withinFamily: This scenario falls within the family target range.
growth.aboveFamily: This scenario falls above the family target range.
growth.unavailable: A valid same-percentile scenario is unavailable for this measurement. The current measurement is still shown.
growth.noMeasurement: This is the population reference chart for the selected sex. To add measured child points and percentiles, select Edit information and enter the child’s measurements. The family target shown above is an adult reference, not a childhood height goal.
growth.scenarioWarning: The dashed line is a conditional illustration, not a prediction. It carries the current height z-score forward through the CDC age curves. Puberty, health and growth tempo can change that path. It does not adjust the family target, use Khamis–Roche or assess bone age.
growth.chartDescription: CDC height reference curves from ages 2 to 20, with entered measurements and an optional dashed same-percentile illustration. Exact values are available in the tables below.
growth.chartHint: On a small screen, scroll the chart sideways. Points are entered measurements; a solid purple line only connects those points. Blue curves are population references.
growth.yearTable: See reference heights for each year (2–20)
growth.tableHint: These are population reference heights, not annual goals or promised growth. The optional scenario appears only at and after the current measurement’s age. All values are rounded.
growth.interpretation: CDC curves describe a US reference population; they are not a personalized Mexican growth standard. A high or low percentile is not a diagnosis. Measurements over time, family heights and clinical assessment provide context. No names or dates of birth are needed for this chart.
growth.source: CDC source data and LMS calculation method
growth.guideTitle: Can a chart show future height each year?
growth.guideText: The optional chart uses the CDC 2000 stature-for-age reference for ages 2–20. Enter the child’s age in completed years plus additional months and their measured standing height. Previous measurements show observed growth. The shaded P3–P97 band describes the reference population; it is not the child’s family target range.
growth.guideScenario: The dashed scenario keeps the current height z-score constant at later ages. For example, a child at the reference median would follow the median curve only if that percentile stayed the same. The age-20 scenario can be compared with the conventional adult family range as a discussion aid. It is not a validated personal adult-height prediction and cannot account for puberty timing, illness or changes in growth velocity. The family target calculation remains based on parental heights and sex.
growth.guideMethod: LMS parameters are linearly interpolated between the surrounding CDC ages. Percentiles come from the corresponding z-score; yearly reference curves and the scenario use the inverse LMS equation. Heights entered in inches are converted to centimeters before calculation.
growth.interactionHint: Hover over the chart or a table row to inspect values. On touch screens, tap. With the chart focused, use ←/→ for months, Shift + ←/→ for years, and Esc to close.
growth.tooltipScenarioHint: Illustration only; not a personal prediction.
growth.topFamilySummary: Estimated adult family target: {value}. Conventional family range: {lower}–{upper}. This is an approximate reference.
growth.scenarioSummaryTitle: Illustration based on the child’s current height
growth.comparisonExplanation: The family target comes from parental heights; the illustration follows the child’s current height percentile. They can give different numbers and neither guarantees the final adult height.
growth.topEndpoint: If the current percentile stayed the same, the reference at age 20 would be approximately <height>{value}</height>.

TargetHeightCalculator.tableBenefitTitle: Yearly height table: compare values alongside the chart
TargetHeightCalculator.tableBenefitText: The yearly height table makes it easier to read and compare numerical values for every age from 2 to 20. Your results show the P3, P50 and P97 CDC stature references for the selected sex, with optional same-percentile illustration values only from the child’s current age onward. Hovering or focusing a row highlights that age on the chart and shows its values. The separate measurements table contains only heights you entered. These tables describe reference values and measurements, not annual height goals or guaranteed growth.
TargetHeightCalculator.publicTableCaption: Yearly CDC median height reference (P50), centimeters
TargetHeightCalculator.publicTableHint: This public table shows population medians for orientation. Complete the calculator to see percentile ranges, entered measurements and the optional illustration together. A median is a reference value, not a recommended height.
TargetHeightCalculator.resultBasis: This calculation uses the parents’ heights and the child’s sex. The child’s current measured height does not change this family reference.

CorrectedAgeCalculator.title: Corrected age calculator for premature babies
CorrectedAgeCalculator.subtitle: Understand your baby’s chronological age, corrected age and postmenstrual age with a visual timeline and a calendar of corrected-age dates.
CorrectedAgeCalculator.seoTitle: Corrected Age Calculator for Premature Babies
CorrectedAgeCalculator.seoDescription: Calculate your premature baby’s corrected, chronological and postmenstrual age. Explore an interactive timeline, age calendar and shareable results.

CorrectedAgeCalculator.monthDay: {months, plural, one {# calendar month} other {# calendar months}} {days, plural, one {# day} other {# days}}

CorrectedAgeCalculator.older: This timeline still shows the arithmetic. Whether to use corrected age for clinical assessment depends on age, purpose and your pediatrician’s guidance.
CorrectedAgeCalculator.calendarHint: These dates mark calendar ages counted from the expected due date. They are not deadlines for developmental skills or a medical appointment schedule.
CorrectedAgeCalculator.calendarCaption: Dates calculated from the expected due date
CorrectedAgeCalculator.nextText: Have weight, length or head circumference measurements? Our growth tools can help you plot them. The appropriate chart and age correction must be chosen for the baby’s age and clinical context.
CorrectedAgeCalculator.intro: A baby born prematurely has a birth date and an expected due date. Chronological age counts time from birth; corrected age counts from the expected due date. Seeing both dates helps explain why a premature baby can have two different age descriptions.
CorrectedAgeCalculator.formula: Corrected age = chronological age − (40 weeks − gestational age at birth)
CorrectedAgeCalculator.formulaText: The calculation uses 40 weeks as its reference point. Enter gestational age as completed weeks plus additional days so that a birth at 32 weeks and 3 days is handled precisely. Postmenstrual age uses a different sum: gestational age at birth plus chronological age.
CorrectedAgeCalculator.exampleText: A baby born at 32 weeks is 8 weeks before the 40-week reference. At 16 weeks after birth, chronological age is 16 weeks, corrected age is 8 weeks, and postmenstrual age is 48 weeks. Weeks are exact seven-day units; calendar months have different lengths.
CorrectedAgeCalculator.visualTitle: A timeline and calendar you can explore
CorrectedAgeCalculator.visualText: The interactive result places birth, the expected due date and your selected assessment date on one timeline. Move the date selector to compare ages on another day, or select a calendar row to explore a corrected-age anniversary. The calendar uses actual calendar months, rather than treating every month as four weeks.
CorrectedAgeCalculator.useText: AAP parent guidance describes using corrected age to understand development during the first two years. Its growth assessment guidance recommends age correction for children born preterm until age three. These are different uses; the calculator does not apply one universal stopping date or assess developmental delay.
CorrectedAgeCalculator.useText2: A birth date and gestational age cannot predict an individual baby’s future weight, length or developmental achievements. Growth charts need actual measurements and a suitable reference. Discuss developmental concerns and the choice of growth chart with the baby’s pediatrician.

difference.q: What is the difference between corrected and chronological age?
difference.a: Chronological age is the time since birth. Corrected age subtracts the interval between birth and the expected due date. Both ages describe the same baby from different starting dates.

negative.q: Why is the result before the due date different?
negative.a: Before the expected due date, the mathematical corrected age is negative. This calculator shows how much time remains until that date instead. Postmenstrual age is still shown in weeks and days.

due.q: Can I calculate corrected age using a due date?
due.a: Yes. Select the expected due date method and enter the original expected date of delivery. The calculator derives the gestational age implied by that date, using the 40-week reference.

months.q: Why are weeks and calendar months different?
months.a: A week always has seven days, but calendar months have 28 to 31 days. The calculator shows exact weeks and days alongside calendar months and days, without using a four-week approximation.

calendar.q: Does the calendar predict when my baby will walk or talk?
calendar.a: No. It only shows when the baby reaches selected corrected calendar ages. Development varies, so these dates are not deadlines for milestones or proof of normal or delayed development.

share.q: Can I share or print the result?
share.a: Yes. Open the result and choose Copy or Print. A link contains the dates used in the calculation and works without an account. Anyone who receives the link can see those dates.
